title: Washing Machine Leaking Water — Causes & Fixes
question: Why is my washing machine leaking water onto the floor?
summary: A washer that leaks onto the floor usually has a loose or worn fill hose, too much detergent or too big a load (oversudsing), a torn or debris-clogged door boot on a front-loader, or a backed-up drain. Most of these are cheap DIY fixes; a tub-seal or bearing leak and control-board faults are where you call an appliance pro.

commonCauses.cause: Loose, worn, or split fill/supply hose connection at the back of the washer — a bad rubber washer or an old rubber hose weeps or bursts. This is the most common leak and a top cause of major home water damage.
commonCauses.quickCheck: Feel the two supply-hose connections and the hoses themselves for wetness; look for crusty mineral buildup, bulging, or cracks in old rubber hoses. A puddle mostly behind the machine points here.

commonCauses.cause: Oversudsing — too much detergent, non-HE detergent in a high-efficiency (HE) washer, or an overloaded drum. Excess suds and sloshing push water out past the seals.
commonCauses.quickCheck: Did you use more than the marked line, or regular detergent in an HE machine? Run a rinse-only cycle; if you see a mound of suds, that is the cause.

commonCauses.cause: Front-loader door boot (rubber bellows) seal is torn, moldy, or trapping coins/hair/debris that break the seal so water sprays out the front during the wash.
commonCauses.quickCheck: Peel back the rubber gasket and look for tears, trapped objects, or gunk. A leak that appears at the front-bottom while it is washing points here.

commonCauses.cause: Clogged or overwhelmed drain — a plugged standpipe, or a drain hose that is loose, cracked, or shoved airtight to the bottom of the standpipe so water backs up and overflows.
commonCauses.quickCheck: Does the leak happen only during drain/spin? Watch the standpipe — if it overflows or the drain hose is wet at its connection, the drain path is the problem.

commonCauses.cause: Clogged coin-trap / drain-pump filter or a cracked, leaking drain pump (common on front-loaders, which have an accessible filter).
commonCauses.quickCheck: Open the small front access panel and check the pump filter for lint and coins; look for water dripping from the pump housing during the drain part of the cycle.

commonCauses.cause: Overfilling from a stuck water inlet valve or failed water-level (pressure) switch, or a worn tub seal/bearing leaking from the center underneath the tub.
commonCauses.quickCheck: If the tub keeps filling past normal, suspect the inlet valve or level switch. If water drips from the center-bottom of the machine (not a hose), the tub seal/bearing is likely — that is a pro job.

fixes: Find the leak first: put dry towels down, run a short cycle, and watch exactly where and when water appears — during fill, wash, or drain/spin. The timing tells you the cause. Unplug the washer before reaching behind or under it.
Fix the detergent and load: use HE detergent (only the marked amount, often just 1-2 tablespoons) in an HE washer and stop overloading. Correct dosing stops oversudsing overflow with zero parts.
Level the machine: a washer that rocks sloshes water and walks. Adjust the leveling feet until it sits solid and level, then re-run a load.

Check and tighten the fill hoses: shut off both water supply valves, look for wet or crusty connections, make sure each fitting has a seated rubber washer, and hand-tighten plus a quarter turn. Replace old rubber hoses with braided stainless-steel ones — they are cheap insurance against a burst that floods a room.
Clean and inspect the door boot (front-loaders): peel back the rubber gasket, wipe the folds, remove coins/hair/debris, and run a clean cycle. If the boot is split or torn, replace it.

Clear the drain path: make sure the drain hose is secured and not pushed airtight to the bottom of the standpipe (it needs an air gap so it can't back-siphon). Snake the standpipe if water backs up during drain.
Clean the drain-pump filter / coin trap (front-loaders): open the small front access panel, set a shallow pan and towels underneath, unscrew the filter to clear lint and coins, then reseat it snugly.

If it overfills or a part has failed: with the washer unplugged and water off, test and replace the water inlet valve or the water-level (pressure) switch. These take a multimeter and some disassembly but are within reach of a confident DIYer.
If water drips from the center underneath the tub (tub seal/bearing), if the control board is suspected, or if you simply cannot find the source, stop and call an appliance technician.
diyVsPro: DIY-safe: hunting down the leak, fixing detergent dose and load size, leveling the machine, tightening or replacing the fill hoses and their washers, cleaning the door boot, clearing the drain and standpipe, and cleaning the drain-pump filter. A confident DIYer can also replace a torn door boot, a drain pump, a water inlet valve, or a level switch after unplugging the machine and shutting off the water. Call a licensed appliance pro for a tub-seal or bearing leak (a major teardown that often costs more than an old machine is worth), a control-board fault, or any time you cannot isolate the source or are not comfortable working around water and power together.
typicalCostUSD: DIY parts: braided stainless-steel fill hoses $10-25 a pair; rubber hose washers $2-5; HE detergent a few dollars; front-load door boot gasket $30-120; drain pump $30-90; water inlet valve $20-60; water-level/pressure switch $15-50. Pro: service call $90-160; common repair $150-400 total including parts; tub seal/bearing replacement $300-500+, which may not be worth it on an older washer.
timeEstimate: Leak-hunting 15-30 min; detergent/leveling/hose fixes 15-40 min; door-boot cleaning ~15 min, full boot replacement 1-2 hrs; clearing a drain or standpipe 30-60 min; pump-filter cleaning 15-30 min; pro visit 1-2 hrs, sometimes a second trip if a part must be ordered.
safetyNote: Unplug the washer and shut off both water supply valves before working on hoses, the pump filter, or any internal part — water and electricity together is a shock and slip hazard. Mop up standing water before you start, and if water has pooled near the outlet or power cord, cut power at the breaker before you step in. A washer runs on a standard 120V outlet (no gas or 240V involved here), but a wet floor around a plugged-in appliance can still shock you. Don't overtighten plastic hose fittings — snug plus a slight turn is enough, or you can crack them. Leave tub-seal/bearing teardown and control-board work to a licensed appliance pro.
toolsParts: Braided stainless-steel fill hoses (to replace old rubber ones)
Replacement front-load door boot gasket (if torn)
Multimeter (to test the inlet valve or level switch)
Replacement drain pump, water inlet valve, or level switch (only if a part has failed)
